app.title: SAEDscope
app.summary: A person loads an electron diffraction pattern, either one file, a 4D-STEM scan reduced to one pattern, a simulated example or several files at once. They then add the elements present and a short description of the sample, and choose how the pattern is calibrated: from the file, from a standard ring pattern, from a scale bar burnt into the image, from typed values, or not at all. A checklist warns about missing elements or calibration and offers one-click fixes. After that, one press of Analyse classifies the pattern as rings, spots or a halo and matches it against candidate phases. The result is a headline verdict with its evidence and flags, an overlay that labels every reflection, ranked candidates, a check against the person's own CIF structures, and a suggested specimen tilt that would separate answers that look alike. The figure, caption, methods paragraph, tables, JSON results and best-matching structure can all be exported.

task.text: Identify which crystal phase and zone axis produced a diffraction pattern, show the evidence for the match, and say what to measure next when several answers fit.

data.text: Diffraction pattern images (one, or a batch) with an optional calibration, matched against a library of reference crystal structures that each predict a list of reflections.

stage.text: indexing diffraction patterns after recording them on the microscope, and checking a phase hypothesis before writing up

mechanism.text: A sidebar of numbered steps collects the pattern, the sample context, the calibration and the candidate sources, and a checklist gates the analysis. The result screen puts a verdict and flags above the pattern with labelled reflections, set next to a simulated zone pattern or a radial profile. Tabs below hold the evidence tables, ranked candidates, a per-structure CIF check, small multiples of what each candidate predicts after a tilt, and the exports.

field.text: selected-area electron diffraction indexing in materials science

workflow.name: identify what produced a measurement by matching it against reference candidates

steps.here: Upload one pattern (.dm3/.dm4/.tif/.png/.npy), reduce a 4D-STEM scan by max, mean or its brightest position, pick a simulated example whose answer is known, or load several files for a batch table

steps.step: narrow the candidates with what is already known
steps.here: Type the elements from EDS and a free-text description, then choose the built-in library, a Materials Project key or your own CIF files; 'Check against my CIF files' switches to testing only your structures

Calibrate from the file, from a standard ring pattern (camera constant and ellipticity are fitted, and a warning shows when the standard came from another camera), from a detected scale bar, from typed Å⁻¹ or nm⁻¹ per pixel, or from voltage and camera length; or leave it uncalibrated

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Analyse pattern finds the centre, classifies the pattern as single crystal, polycrystal or amorphous, and matches rings or spots. The verdict names the phase and zone axis with errors, and the overlay labels each reflection

steps.step: compare the result against the person's own references
steps.here: Each uploaded CIF gets a verdict (consistent, lattice change, scale mismatch, partly, not consistent), with predicted and measured reflections side by side and a refined cell; the Candidates tab ranks every phase

steps.step: plan the next measurement that would settle it
steps.here: Next step lists specimen tilts within ±35° and draws what each candidate would show after the tilt; for ring patterns it lists the rings one candidate has and the other lacks
Download the figure (PNG), results (JSON), reflection table (CSV) and best phase (CIF), with a drafted figure caption and methods paragraph; batch mode downloads one CSV row per file

distinctive: The calibration is treated as suspect: the tool reports when the best match fits only at a scale several percent off, and when a standard was recorded on another camera, binning or camera length
Phases whose lattices are too close to separate are named together as a look-alike group rather than one being guessed, and the person is asked for elements or a calibration
When several answers fit, it simulates what each would show after the same specimen tilt, so the person knows which tilt will tell them apart
Pattern type (single crystal, polycrystal, amorphous, or one systematic row) is decided first and changes which right-hand view and evidence table appear
A language model only rewords the computed numbers into an explanation; the matching itself is diffraction physics
